newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Survey shows Czechs prefer EU to NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Survey shows Czechs prefer EU to NATO membership.

text.p: A majority of Czechs favour membership in the European Union, but less than half wish to become part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation a poll released on Tuesday showed.

The survey, conducted by the private public opinion agency Factum over the first 10 days of December 1996, showed 55 percent backed the country's membership of the EU while only 37 percent agreed with its membership in NATO.
Conversely, 17 percent of the 1,074 respondents said they were against membership in the EU, while 32 percent are against the country's inclusion in the western security alliance.
The number of undecided respondents was very similiar -- 28 percent as regards the EU and 31 percent when it comes to NATO.
The Czechs, along with the Poles and the Hungarians, are widely seen as top candidates for the planned expansion of both the EU and NATO.

A survey by the state-funded Institute for Public Opinion Research (IVVM) conducted in November 1996 showed 38 percent of Czechs support becoming one of the first former Soviet Bloc countries to join NATO, while 35 percent oppose it.
While Czech politicians generally agree there must a referendum on the EU membership, they still are mixed on whether there should also be one on NATO membership.

The centre-right ruling coalition parties -- the Civic Democratic Party of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, along with the junior Civic Democratic Aliance and Christian Democratic Union -- are all against a referendum on the issue.
The strongest opposition party, the Social Democrats (CSSD), supports joining the alliance, but insists on a plebiscite to confirm the country's desire for membership.
Two other minor opposition parties, the Communists and the ultra-right Republicans are firmly against any plans for Czech membership in either body.
